title: Cheese
text:
Show the code
cheeses <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2024/2024-06-04/cheeses.csv')


About the data:
The data for this analysis come from the TidyTuesday Cheese dataset.
About the dataset:
This dataset comes from cheese.com. Cheese.com is an online database containing information about cheese from all around the globe. They have data around the specific ingredients for each cheese, what wines pair well with each cheese, and photos of all the cheeses. This dataset in particular contains information on 1187 different cheeses, from their country of origin to the fat content of the cheese.
Citation:
Cheese.com - World’s Greatest Cheese Resource. (2019). Cheese.Com. https://www.cheese.com/
Tidy Analysis:


Show the code
library(tidyverse)

cheeses2 <- cheeses |>
  filter(!is.na(rind)) |>
  group_by(rind) |>
  summarise(num_cheeses = n()) |>
  mutate(percent = num_cheeses / sum(num_cheeses) * 100)

ggplot(cheeses2, aes(x = reorder(rind, percent), y = percent)) +
    coord_flip() +
    geom_col() +
    labs(
        title = "Percentage of Cheeses by Rind Type",
        x = "Rind",
        y = "Percentage of Cheeses"
    )









This bar chart shows what percent of all cheeses in the dataset have each type of rind. As shown in the chart, about half of all the cheeses in this dataset have natural rinds, and cheeses with edible rinds make up the smallest percentage of this dataset.

title: Netflix Title Analysis
text:
Introduction
Movie and TV show titles are the first things users look at when trying to decide what to watch on streaming platforms like Netflix. While titles are often short, they are meant to draw audiences in, convince them to watch a movie/show, and hint at what the movie might be about. Thus, my first visualization explores the most frequent words that appear in titles across genres. Specifically, I am looking at 15 genres: Action, Comedy, Drama, Horror, Romance, Sci-Fi, Fantasy, Thriller, Mystery, Documentaries, Musical, Crime, Children, International, and Miscellaneous.
Next, I will look at how title vocabulary changed before and during Covid-19. Specifically, I want to see whether words that center around disease, death, isolation, and other pandemic-related imagery were more common in movie titles before and during Covid.

title: Netflix Title Analysis
text:
About the Data
The data for this analysis come from the TidyTuesday Netflix Titles dataset.

About the Dataset
This dataset comes from Kaggle and was uploaded to the website by Shivam Bansal. The dataset consists of movies and TV shows available on Netflix as of 2020. Additionally, the dataset has been collected from Flixable, a third-party Netflix search engine.
This database contains information on 7787 movies/TV shows on Netflix, from each show’s title to their cast, rating, and release date.

title: Netflix Title Analysis
text:
Data Analysis


Show the code
#Creating a subset of the netflix_titles dataset
cleaned_titles <- netflix_titles |>
    select(show_id, type, title, listed_in, release_year) |>
    filter(!is.na(title), !is.na(listed_in)) |>
    separate_rows(listed_in, sep = ", ") |>
    separate_rows(listed_in, sep = "& ")

#Adding variables and formatting the cleaned_titles dataset
cleaned_titles <- cleaned_titles |>
    mutate(listed_in = str_to_lower(listed_in)) |> #string function 1
    mutate(genre = ifelse(
            str_detect(listed_in, "action") | str_detect(listed_in, "adventure"), "Action", #string function 2

            ifelse(str_detect(listed_in, "comed"), "Comedy",

            ifelse(str_detect(listed_in, "drama"), "Drama",

            ifelse(str_detect(listed_in, "horror"), "Horror",

            ifelse(str_detect(listed_in, "romant"), "Romance",

            ifelse(str_detect(listed_in, "sci-fi"), "Sci-Fi",

            ifelse(str_detect(listed_in, "fantasy"), "Fantasy",

            ifelse(str_detect(listed_in, "thriller"), "Thriller",

            ifelse(str_detect(listed_in, "myster"), "Mystery",

            ifelse(str_detect(listed_in, "docu") | str_detect(listed_in, "nature") | str_detect(listed_in, "science"), "Documentary",

            ifelse(str_detect(listed_in, "music"), "Musical",

            ifelse(str_detect(listed_in, "crime"), "Crime",

            ifelse(str_detect(listed_in, "children") | str_detect(listed_in, "kid") | str_detect(listed_in, "teen") | str_detect(listed_in, "family"), "Children", 

            ifelse(str_detect(listed_in, "international") | str_detect(listed_in, "british") | str_detect(listed_in, "korean") | str_detect(listed_in, "spanish"), "International",
            "Miscellaneous"))))))))))))))
        )

title: Netflix Title Analysis
text:
Visualization 1


Show the code
#filler words that need to be excluded
stop_words <- c("the", "and", "for", "with", "you", "your", "are", "was", "but", "not", "from", "this", "that", "his", "her", "its", "our", "out", "one", "two", "of", "in", "to", "my", "la", "el", "on", "de", "be")

#splitting the titles into individual words and cleaning them up
title_words <- cleaned_titles |>
    separate_rows(title, sep = "\\s+") |> #regex 1
    mutate(word = str_to_lower(title), word = str_replace_all(word, "[^a-z]", "")) |> #3rd string function! and 2nd regex
    filter(str_detect(title, "(?<![A-Za-z])[A-Za-z]{2,}(?![A-Za-z])"), word != "", !word %in% stop_words #regex 3 and lookaround!
    )


#finding the top 3 words for each genre
top_words <- title_words |>
    mutate(genre = as.factor(genre)) |>
    count(genre, word, name = "frequency") |>
    group_by(genre) |>
    arrange(desc(frequency), word) |>
    mutate(rank = row_number()) |>
    filter(rank <= 3) |>
    mutate(genre = fct_relevel(genre, c("Action", "Family", "Comedy", "Crime", "Documentary", "Drama", "Horror", "International", "Musical", "Mystery", "Romance", "Sci-Fi & Fantasy", "Thriller", "Miscellaneous"))) #factor function!


#making the plot
ggplot(top_words, aes(x = word, y = frequency)) +
    geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
    coord_flip() +
    facet_wrap(~ genre, scales = "free") +
    labs(
        title = "Three Most Frequent Words in Netflix Titles by Genre",
        subtitle = "Common filler words excluded",
        x = "Word",
        y = "Frequency in Titles",
        ) +
    theme_minimal()









For this first visualization, I wanted to see how the most frequent words in movie/TV show titles differed across the various genres I chose. To do so, I sorted each of the 42 “listed_in” categories in the original dataset into 14 genres (Action, Comedy, Drama, Horror, Romance, Sci-Fi & Fantasy, Thriller, Mystery, Documentaries, Musical, Crime, Family, International, and Miscellaneous) and identified the top 3 words that appeared in movie titles within all of these genres.
Some of the results I found were expected, such as with the crime genre’s most popular words in titles (“murder”, “killer”, and “crime”) or with the words in the documentary genre (“world”, “story”, “life”). Additionally, there are words that appear throughout many genres, like “love” and “christmas”. However, the visual also shows us that many of the genres have titles with unintuitive words. For example, “black” is a word that shows up in many tites across genres, but I can’t think of why that is.
Ultimately, looking at this visual, it is clear that the connotations of words are considered when creating titles across genres. For example, words like “christmas” evoke feelings of comfort and joy, and these words are most frequently in romance, comedy, and family titles. On the other hand, words like “murder” and “killer” in movie/TV show titles suggest the title will be a crime-related story, and words like “house” and “dark” used in combination can suggest a horror/thriller title.

title: Edible Plants
text:
About the dataset
The dataset comes from the Edible Plant Database (EPD). The EPD is an outcome of the GROW Observatory, a European Citizen Science project focused on growing food, monitoring land, and sensing soil moisture. This database contains information on 146 edible plant species, from each plant’s idea growing conditions to their time to harvest and germination.

Citation
Edible Plant Database. (n.d.). Edible Plant Database. https://edibleplantdb.org/
